findings.claim: Jones, Evidence-Based Software Engineering (slug 003) — empirical research on what practices correlate with what outcomes; MCDP-1 is the doctrinal frame the research findings often confirm.
findings.failure_mode: Misstates the other source. Jones's deep ref says the evidence base is close to empty and his own models are post-hoc; it confirms no doctrinal frame, and MCDP-1 is nowhere in it.
findings.evidence: Jones deep 13: "evidence-based software engineering is essentially a blank slate" [V]; deep 17: "the almost non-existent evidence for current theories of software development" [V]; "just-so stories created from a fishing expedition" [V].
findings.fix: correct: Jones, Evidence-Based Software Engineering (slug 003): the empirical check. Jones finds the evidence base for software practices thin; treat MCDP-1's transfers (tempo, main effort, mission tactics) as hypotheses his data rarely tests.

findings.claim: Humble & Farley (Continuous Delivery): deployment frequency is the most-correlated DORA metric; shipping faster is competing on OODA tempo.
findings.failure_mode: Training-data claim about a source not held in the demo corpus, and misattributed: DORA metrics are not from Continuous Delivery, and 'most-correlated' is an unsourced figure.
findings.evidence: No demo deep ref mentions DORA or deployment frequency; Humble & Farley appear only in the MCDP-1 deep ref's list of another corpus's slugs (deep 227).
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Beck (XP): weekly cycle, quarterly cycle — the cadences are designed to outpace the requirements-change cycle.
findings.failure_mode: Training-data claim about a source not held in the demo corpus; the design rationale is asserted without any reference.
findings.evidence: Beck appears in the MCDP-1 deep ref only at 227 (another corpus's slug 071); no demo deep ref carries XP's weekly/quarterly cycles.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Steve Blank (Customer Development): customer-development tempo determines time-to-product-market-fit.
findings.failure_mode: Training-data claim; the only demo mention of Blank is his problem-solution fit in the Entrepreneurship deep ref, with no tempo claim.
findings.evidence: OpenStax Entrepreneurship deep 295: "The chapter cites Steve Blank's problem-solution-fit"; nothing on tempo or customer development.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: ... what high-performing software companies operationalise as one big bet per quarter.
findings.failure_mode: Empirical claim about high performers with no source.
findings.evidence: No deep ref in the corpus carries this; MCDP-1 deep 146 describes main effort only.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Architectural runway in agile architecture (the framing within which teams make local technology decisions).
findings.failure_mode: Outside concept not held in the corpus and described loosely (in SAFe it names existing technical enablement, not a decision frame); the only 'runway' in the corpus is cash runway.
findings.evidence: OpenStax Entrepreneurship deep 271: runway = cash on hand / monthly burn. No other demo deep ref mentions architectural runway.
findings.fix: strip

findings.section: Software / Business Relevance, thread 5 (Surfaces and gaps)
findings.claim: Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm / Clayton Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma / Blue Ocean Strategy all operationalise versions of this.
findings.failure_mode: Moore and Blue Ocean are not held in the corpus; no reference states the relationship. Christensen is held only through the Entrepreneurship deep ref's disruptive-innovation summary.
findings.evidence: OpenStax Entrepreneurship deep 119, 301: Christensen's disruptive innovation (entrants target overlooked segments or nonconsumers). No demo deep ref mentions Crossing the Chasm or Blue Ocean.
findings.fix: correct: Christensen's disruptive innovation, as summarised in OpenStax Entrepreneurship (slug 00f, Ch 11.1), is a close business analogue: entrants go where incumbents are not looking, turning nonconsumers into consumers or targeting overlooked segments.

findings.section: Software / Business Relevance, thread 6 (Severity on inaction)
findings.claim: This is the operational form of Edmondson's psychological safety (and connects to the resilience-engineering corollary: practitioners create safety only when permitted to act).
findings.failure_mode: Edmondson is not held in the corpus; the resilience-engineering point comes from Cook, a source in another corpus. Equating severity toward inaction with psychological safety is also in tension with the corpus's own psychological-safety material (blameless, safe to speak up).
findings.evidence: No demo deep ref mentions Edmondson. MCDP-1 deep 221 cites Cook Point 17 as slug 076 of the AARBuddy corpus. OPL deep 101-110: psychological safety built by rituals (check-ins, blameless conversation structures).
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: MCDP-1 is the doctrinal application of John Boyd's strategic theory — particularly the OODA loop and the concept of operating inside the adversary's decision cycle.
findings.failure_mode: Overstates Boyd's place: the deep ref names Clausewitz as the explicit philosophical companion throughout (cited 14 times) and Boyd in two notes. 'Operating inside the adversary's decision cycle' is not a phrase or concept the deep ref carries.
findings.evidence: Deep 15: Clausewitz "the explicit philosophical companion throughout, cited 14 times"; deep 43: OODA "named once, in Notes 18 of Ch 2, but the underlying logic saturates Chs 2 and 4"; deep 198: Boyd cited at Notes 18 of Ch 2 and Notes 5 of Ch 4.
findings.fix: correct: MCDP-1 is the Marine Corps' maneuver-warfare doctrine, built on Clausewitz and carrying John Boyd's tempo logic: it names the OODA loop at Notes 18 of Ch 2, and the logic runs through Chs 2 and 4.

findings.claim: The OODA-loop claim — the side that completes the cycle faster, or that operates in a way the adversary cannot orient to, wins.
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref's thesis-heading wording stated as the doctrinal claim; 'operates in a way the adversary cannot orient to' is not in the source and 'wins' overstates.
findings.evidence: Deep 43 [V] (Notes 18 of Ch 2): "the party who consistently completes the cycle faster gains an advantage that increases with each cycle."
findings.fix: correct: The OODA-loop claim, that "the party who consistently completes the cycle faster gains an advantage that increases with each cycle" [V] (Notes 18 of Ch 2), is the doctrinal statement of tempo as strategy.

findings.claim: Eric Ries (Lean Startup): Build-Measure-Learn cycle speed determines the rate of validated learning.
findings.failure_mode: The build-measure-learn loop is held (via OpenStax Entrepreneurship); the claim that cycle speed determines the rate of validated learning is not.
findings.evidence: OpenStax Entrepreneurship deep 17: "continuous validation through the build-measure-learn loop, drawn from Eric Ries's Lean Startup"; deep 261: "continuously testing their products and getting feedback from customers in real time."
findings.fix: correct: Eric Ries (Lean Startup, via OpenStax Entrepreneurship, slug 00f): continuous testing and customer feedback through the build-measure-learn loop.

findings.claim: Main effort / Schwerpunkt (Ch 4); 'your Schwerpunkt discipline is missing' (line 27).
findings.failure_mode: The source's term is 'main effort'; 'Schwerpunkt' comes from the deep ref's [AR] note.
findings.evidence: Deep 146 [AR]; source: no occurrence of 'Schwerpunkt'.
findings.fix: correct: replace 'Schwerpunkt' with 'main effort' at lines 23, 27 and 66.

findings.claim: The discipline of one main effort is the doctrinal version of what Goldratt teaches (Theory of Constraints: identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it).
findings.failure_mode: Traces to the deep ref's own connection, which it marks [AR]; the distillation drops the marker and presents the equivalence as fact. Goldratt is not held as a primary in this corpus (Open Kanban cites him only for the holistic-system value).
findings.evidence: Deep 146: "[AR — Goldratt's Theory of Constraints names this as identifying the one constraint to act on ...]"; Open Kanban deep 52, 131: Goldratt [BT] for holistic view.
findings.fix: re-mark: [AR]; correct: [AR] The one-main-effort discipline parallels Goldratt's Theory of Constraints (identify the constraint; subordinate everything else to it). Goldratt is not held in this corpus; Open Kanban (slug 008) cites him for the holistic-system view.

findings.claim: The OKR system (Objectives = intent; Key Results = measurable execution within intent).
findings.failure_mode: Mapping conflicts with the corpus's own OKR definition: the Open Practice Library defines the Objective as 'the what' and the Key Result as 'the how', whereas MCDP-1's intent is the why.
findings.evidence: OPL deep 174 [V]: "The Objective - The what. The Key Result - The how"; MCDP-1 deep 144 [V]: "The task denotes what is to be done ... the intent explains why."
findings.fix: correct: The OKR system (Open Practice Library, slug 009), with a caution: OKRs define the Objective as the what, so the intent (the why) has to be stated alongside it for the parallel to hold.

findings.claim: The pamphlet's disciplinary requirement — intent must be understood two levels up.
findings.failure_mode: Hardens 'should understand ... at least two levels up'.
findings.evidence: Deep 144 [V] (Ch 4, "Commander's intent").
findings.fix: correct: The pamphlet's guidance that subordinates "should understand the intent of the commander at least two levels up" [V] (Ch 4, "Commander's intent").

findings.claim: If your team does not know the intent two levels up, the question is not can they be trusted? — it is have we communicated the intent clearly enough?
findings.failure_mode: One-sided: the source puts the burden of understanding on senior and subordinate alike.
findings.evidence: Source 3761-3766 (Ch 4, "Commander's intent"): "The burden of understanding falls on senior and subordinate alike." Deep 142: the subordinate is obligated to act in conformity with the intent.
findings.fix: correct: If your team does not know the intent two levels up, ask both halves of MCDP-1's shared burden (Ch 4, "Commander's intent"): have we stated the intent clearly, and has the team sought it?

findings.claim: Surfaces and gaps (Ch 2)
findings.failure_mode: Mis-cited chapter: surfaces and gaps is Ch 4.
findings.evidence: Deep 148 (Ch 4, "Surfaces and gaps").
findings.fix: correct: Surfaces and gaps (Ch 4)

findings.claim: The asymmetry of consequences is the structural condition for any culture of experimentation, learning, or psychological safety. Errors of commission should be tolerated; errors of omission should be the punishable failure mode.
findings.failure_mode: Broadens leniency from errors of overboldness to all errors of commission and drops the source's limits (constructive criticism still applies; no licence for reckless acts). 'Psychological safety' is not in the MCDP-1 deep ref.
findings.evidence: Deep 109 [V] (Ch 3, "Professionalism"); source 2398-2401: "constructive criticism is an important element in learning. Nor does it give subordinates free license to act stupidly or recklessly."
findings.fix: correct: The asymmetry of consequences is a structural condition for a culture of experimentation: errors that come from acting boldly (we shipped, it failed, we learned) are treated leniently as part of learning; errors of inaction or timidity are dealt with severely (Ch 3, "Professionalism"). Leniency is not licence for recklessness.

findings.claim: The OODA / Schwerpunkt / mission-tactics / surfaces-and-gaps machinery transfers; the Zweikampf framing usually does not.
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref treats the clash of wills as the foundation of tempo and OODA; relative speed and surfaces/gaps presuppose an opposing will, so they cannot be cleanly split from it.
findings.evidence: Deep 37 [AR]: interacting wills "is the foundation for every later move toward tempo, mission tactics, and the OODA loop"; deep 91: "it is relative speed that matters"; deep 148: gaps are enemy weaknesses.
findings.fix: correct: Main effort and mission tactics transfer most readily. OODA tempo and surfaces-and-gaps assume an opposing will; name the competitor or market dynamic that plays that role before applying them. The pure Zweikampf framing usually does not transfer.

findings.claim: The doctrine's emphasis on tempo as decisive needs calibration ... Some markets reward fastest-mover; others reward last-correct-mover.
findings.failure_mode: Overstates the doctrine to set up the caution: MCDP-1 calls tempo 'often the most important' weapon, stresses relative not absolute speed, and counts calculated patience as boldness. The market typology is the distillation's own unsourced judgement.
findings.evidence: Deep 87 [V]: "Tempo is itself a weapon — often the most important"; deep 91 [V]: "it is relative speed that matters rather than absolute speed"; deep 93 [V]: "A nervy, calculating patience that allows the enemy to commit himself irrevocably before we strike him can also be a form of boldness."
findings.fix: correct: MCDP-1 already qualifies tempo: it is "often the most important" weapon, it is relative speed that matters, and "a nervy, calculating patience" can be boldness [V] (Ch 2). [AR] In markets dominated by network effects, switching costs or regulatory inertia, weigh that patience clause as heavily as the speed clause.

notes: Hash matches current deep ref. The file does not follow the nine-section template and carries no [V] quotes (source is Scope: open). The main pattern is training-data leakage in the 'doctrinal version of' lists: Humble & Farley/DORA, Beck/XP, Blank, architectural runway, Moore, Blue Ocean and Edmondson are not held in the demo corpus. Several connections (Boyd lineage, Marquet, Goldratt) trace only to the MCDP-1 deep ref's 'Connections to corpus' section, which names slugs from the AARBuddy corpus rather than this one; Marquet (line 33) was graded FAITHFUL because it traces to deep 223, but that deep-ref claim ('the doctrinal lineage flows directly from MCDP 1') is itself unmarked and worth an upstream check.
